 After the Malaysian Grand Prix, Bagnaia revealed to Sky that during testing at Misano and Motegi in 2025, he had regained his competitiveness thanks to a technical modification that has since been removed. But Tardozzi replied, “I have no idea what he’s referring to.”  
 Two World Championships won together, a bike that continues to win with Márquez, and a problem that no one has been able to solve for nearly two years. What’s going on in the Ducati garage?
 Read more 
 MotoGP Bagnaia: “I’m counting down the minutes until the end of this season.” 
 There’s a mystery, and it doesn’t involve an aerodynamic component, a new frame, or an engine upgrade. Or maybe it does. Because, judging by the statements made by Francesco Bagnaia and Davide Tardozzi after the Malaysian Grand Prix, the issue is not merely understanding why Pecco can no longer ride the Desmosedici as he would like. The even more surprising problem is that rider and team do not even appear to share the same interpretation of what happened.
 Follow 
 For a structure that has dominated MotoGP in recent years, this is perhaps the most troubling aspect.
 Bagnaia: The Modification That Gave Me Back the Ducati
 His words are precise, and above all, they introduce a new element into a saga that has been dragging on for nearly two seasons now. “During the Misano test and the 2025 Japanese Grand Prix , something other than simple adjustments and setup changes were altered. That change allowed me to ride again. Now that thing doesn’t exist, just as it no longer existed after last year’s race in Japan…” 
Let’s pause on this declaration, because it contains at least three important points.
 The first is that Bagnaia explicitly distinguishes between normal bike adjustments and a modification of a different nature. He is not, therefore, simply talking about preload, geometry, electronics, or balance—at least not in the sense of routine tuning operations.
 Podcast 
 The second is that, according to Pecco, that modification had worked . It hadn’t just improved his lap time—it had given him back the ability to ride. A substantial difference for a rider who has built his success on precise braking, corner entry, and the ability to make the most of the Ducati’s front end.
 Read more 
 MotoGP Bagnaia: "When I look at the data from my riding, I don't even recognise myself any more" 
 The third point is perhaps the most intriguing: that solution disappeared after Motegi 2025 and is no longer available today. 
 Why? Was it a technical decision? Was it due to regulatory reasons? Was it because it couldn’t be replicated? Or was it because what Bagnaia had perceived as a decisive change wasn’t actually attributable to a single component?
 These are questions to which, for the moment, there is no verified answer.
 Tardozzi: We’ve tried everything; we’re at a dead end
 While Bagnaia’s words raise the mystery, those of Davide Tardozzi make it even more complicated. Speaking to Sky TV, the Ducati team manager acknowledged a situation that would have been hard to imagine back when Pecco won his two world titles. “Whatever we’ve done lately—and even over the past year or so—hasn’t improved Bagnaia’s performance. We’re aware that he’s a champion and has innate speed, but right now not even his crew chief and his electronics specialist—with whom he won two World Championships—have a clear path forward. We’ve explored every possibility, and we’re at an impasse.” 
 It’s a weighty admission. Because it doesn’t come from a team struggling with an uncompetitive bike, but from MotoGP’s technical benchmark. And because it directly involves the people who know Bagnaia better than anyone else—those who accompanied him in winning his two championships.
 Tardozzi emphasizes one point : “I’ve always said that we’ll never stop helping him. We’ve even done things tailored exclusively to him, but unfortunately, we still haven’t found what he needs.” 
So Ducati hasn’t stood still. It has worked, experimented, and developed specific solutions. But none have produced the desired result.
 Ducati itself wins with Márquez. So what?
 There’s also another factor that makes the Bagnaia situation particularly difficult to interpret: the Desmosedici’s competitiveness in the hands of other riders . “The bike is the same one he used to achieve those results. It’s the same one Marc won with today and the one Alex used to get on the podium. We have no idea what’s going on.” 
 Tardozzi points out a fact: Ducati continues to be a winner. Marc Márquez manages to make the most of it, Alex Márquez is competitive, while Bagnaia continues to search for a feeling that seems out of reach.
 But here we must be careful not to fall into a misconception.
Two technically identical bikes are not necessarily two bikes that provide the same feeling to their respective riders.
Riding style, front-brake management, how the tyre is loaded, and the ability to adapt to certain bike movements can transform a technical characteristic into an advantage for one rider and a limitation for another.
 Read more 
 MotoGP Bagnaia: “Team orders? I’ve never asked for or received any assistance.” 
 Márquez, after all, has repeatedly demonstrated his ability to adapt to bikes with challenging handling characteristics. Bagnaia, on the other hand, has built his speed on an extremely precise relationship with the front end.
 This doesn’t mean that one is necessarily better than the other. It means that the same motorcycle can offer very different performance margins depending on who’s riding it.
 Yet an explanation based solely on riding style isn’t enough to solve the mystery. Bagnaia claims that, on at least two occasions in 2025, the solution was found.
 The most surprising statement: “I have no idea what he’s referring to” 
 And here we are at the crux of the matter.
When asked specifically about the technical change mentioned by Bagnaia, Tardozzi replied: “In all honesty, I have no idea what he’s referring to.” 
 It’s probably the most significant statement of the entire affair.
Because here we’re not talking about a difference of opinion regarding performance, nor about a rider asking for a different bike than the one the engineers consider best.
 We’re talking about a rider who identifies a specific technical change—at least based on his own riding experience—and his team manager who claims not to know what he’s referring to.
 Of course, this doesn’t mean that Ducati’s engineers are unaware of the modifications made during the Misano tests and the Motegi weekend. Every technical adjustment is normally documented, analyzed, and compared with the collected data. 
 And Tardozzi, as team manager, may not be privy to every detail of the configurations being tested.
But the gap between the two statements remains evident.
 Bagnaia seems to be saying: I know when we found the solution, and I know it’s gone now. 
 Tardozzi responds, essentially: we don’t know what the solution is, and we don’t even know which change you’re referring to. 
It’s a contradiction that deserves clarification.
 Misano and Motegi 2025: Two Clues to Build On
 At this point, perhaps, the question Ducati should be asking itself is no longer just how to make Bagnaia competitive again.
 The question is: what was different about his bike between the Misano test and the 2025 Japanese Grand Prix? 
 If these really weren’t just standard adjustments, the range of possibilities could include chassis components, different structural configurations, changes to the ergonomics, or other solutions capable of altering the Desmosedici’s dynamic behavior.
 However, there isn’t enough evidence to pinpoint a specific modification, and it would be wrong to turn a hypothesis into a certainty.
There’s also another possibility: that the improvement stemmed from the interaction of multiple factors and that Bagnaia identified as decisive a change which, when taken out of context, doesn’t produce the same effects. 
 But precisely for this reason, comparing the technical configurations used on those occasions could be crucial.
The aim would not be to seek a miracle solution, but to understand whether there is a verifiable relationship between a technical adjustment and the rider’s restored riding feel.
 The issue is not purely technical—it is also one of confidence.
 After nearly two years of difficulties, it would be naive to imagine that Bagnaia’s problem has remained confined to the mechanicals of the bike.
A rider who can no longer trust the front, who must constantly adjust his riding style, and who sees his teammate winning on a substantially identical bike inevitably ends up losing his bearings.
 And when those bearings are lost, even technical changes become harder to evaluate. 
 The risk is entering a vicious cycle: the rider lacks confidence, asks for changes, the team implements them, results don’t materialize, and every subsequent attempt becomes harder to interpret.
 However, it would be a mistake to reverse the cause-and-effect relationship.
 Attributing everything to a psychological issue would be an oversimplification . A loss of confidence can be a consequence of technical difficulties, not necessarily their cause.
 And above all, it wouldn’t explain why Bagnaia has identified two specific moments when he claims to have rediscovered his bike.
Two World Championships together. And now they don’t understand each other anymore?
Finally, there’s a human and organizational aspect that cannot be overlooked.
 Bagnaia and Ducati are not strangers forced to learn how to work together; they have won two World Championships, developed a proven working methodology, and weathered difficult times before achieving success.
The crew chief and the electronics specialist know his demands, his language, and his reactions.
 That is precisely why it is surprising that, after so many months, the team admits to lacking a clear direction.
This is not about assigning blame; it is about understanding how a technical and human system that once worked so effectively has lost the ability to interpret the rider’s needs.
 Ducati has proven it can build a winning bike, and Bagnaia has proven he can win on that bike. Yet today, those two certainties no longer align.
 The real mystery isn’t why Bagnaia is riding slowly
 Perhaps that is precisely the point.
The mystery isn’t that a rider—even a two-time world champion—might go through a rough patch. It has happened many times in the history of motorcycle racing.
 The mystery is that Bagnaia claims to have already found, at least temporarily, the answer to his problem, and that Ducati, more than a year later, has been unable to devise an effective solution. 
Or, at the very least, that’s the impression that emerges from the words of the two protagonists.
 Pecco says there was something there, and now it’s gone. 
 Tardozzi says he doesn’t know what Pecco is referring to. 
One is looking for something he claims to have already had. The other keeps searching for something he still can’t identify.
This is perhaps the starkest snapshot of Ducati’s situation: not a motorcycle that has stopped winning, but a team and a champion who, after speaking the same language for years, now seem unable to understand one another.
 And until it is clarified what really happened between Misano and Motegi 2025, the Bagnaia case will remain a mystery— not just regarding performance, but also regarding approach, communication, and trust.
